Week 07 / Screen-by-screen walkthrough

One action at a time, from an extracted ZIP to a deployed API.

This guide pairs real interface captures with exact actions, expected results, and recovery checks. Click any screenshot to open a larger view. Use Escape or Close to return.

Capture scope: the app and Swagger requests ran locally. GitHub and Render captures show real creation forms before submission. Neon’s connection-dialog image comes from its official documentation. A completed public cloud deployment is not claimed.

01 / Download and extract the complete practice project

01 / Setup

Where to begin

Lecture HTML: press R, or open slide “Your practice files”.

Do this, in order

  1. Choose Complete practice project. Save Week07_Practice.zip in a folder you can find again, such as Downloads.
  2. Windows: right-click the ZIP and choose Extract All. macOS: double-click the ZIP. Open the extracted campus-board folder.
  3. All features are implemented. No source edits are required. Working inside the ZIP viewer does not edit an extracted project.
  4. Open VS Code. Choose File > Open Folder and select campus-board. The Explorer should show backend, frontend, Dockerfile, README.md, and scripts.

Expected result

Both backend/pom.xml and frontend/package.json are visible inside one campus-board root.

If your screen differs

If VS Code shows another campus-board folder as its only child, open that child instead. If files are read-only, extract the ZIP first.

02 / Check the tools before opening two terminals

01 / Setup

Where to begin

VS Code: Terminal > New Terminal.

Do this, in order

  1. Use the installation commands for your operating system in the lecture’s setup chapter. Install JDK 21 and Node 24 LTS, then reopen VS Code.
  2. Run each version command below. Both java and javac must work. npm should arrive with Node. Git is needed for the later push.
  3. The sample also supports JDK 17. Use the recommended versions for a consistent class setup. Do not install Maven separately: backend/mvnw and mvnw.cmd supply it.
  4. If java works but javac does not, install a JDK rather than only a JRE. If versions stay old, reopen the terminal and check PATH/JAVA_HOME.

Copyable input or command

java -version
javac -version
node --version
npm --version
git --version

Expected result

Each command prints a version, not “command not found” or “not recognized”.

If your screen differs

On Windows, use PowerShell. Inside WSL, use Linux Java and Node together rather than mixing Windows and WSL executables.

03 / Prepare the included Maven Wrapper

01 / Setup

Where to begin

A terminal in the extracted campus-board folder, after installing JDK 21.

Do this, in order

  1. Maven builds Java projects and downloads their dependencies. Maven Wrapper is a project launcher: mvnw on macOS/Linux and mvnw.cmd on Windows. It downloads Maven 3.9.11 on first use; you do not install mvnw globally.
  2. Run cd backend. Use ls -a on macOS/Linux or Get-ChildItem -Force in PowerShell. Check pom.xml, mvnw, mvnw.cmd, and .mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties. The .mvn directory is hidden; keep it when copying the project.
  3. macOS/Linux: run chmod +x mvnw, then ./mvnw --version. Windows PowerShell: run .\mvnw.cmd --version. Choose only the block for your operating system.
  4. Wait for the initial download. Confirm Apache Maven 3.9.11 and Java version 21 (17 is also supported). This prepares Maven; the Spring Boot command downloads the application dependencies next.
  5. If wrapper files are missing, re-extract the complete Practice ZIP into a separate folder and restore mvnw, mvnw.cmd, and .mvn into your existing backend without replacing your edited source files.

Copyable input or command

# macOS / Linux — start in campus-board
cd backend
ls -a
ls .mvn/wrapper
chmod +x mvnw
./mvnw --version

# Windows PowerShell — start in campus-board instead
cd backend
Get-ChildItem -Force
Get-ChildItem .mvn/wrapper
.\mvnw.cmd --version

Expected result

The version command prints Apache Maven 3.9.11 and the installed JDK version, then returns to the prompt.

If your screen differs

Permission denied: from backend run chmod +x mvnw. No such file / command not recognized: confirm the directory and use ./mvnw or .\mvnw.cmd, including the prefix. JAVA_HOME error: run java -version and javac -version, fix the JDK path, and reopen the terminal. Download error: check internet or proxy settings, then retry. This only-script wrapper needs no maven-wrapper.jar.

Official reference: https://maven.apache.org/tools/wrapper/

04 / Start Terminal A and leave it running

01 / Setup

Where to begin

Terminal A, starting in campus-board.

Do this, in order

  1. Run cd backend. In this directory, ls (macOS/Linux) or dir (PowerShell) should show pom.xml and the wrapper files.
  2. macOS/Linux: run chmod +x mvnw once, then ./mvnw spring-boot:run. Windows: run .\mvnw.cmd spring-boot:run.
  3. Wait while Maven downloads dependencies. The first run takes longer. A running server keeps the terminal occupied; this is normal.
  4. Find “Started BoardApplication” and the port 18707. Keep this terminal running. Open a second terminal with the + button for Vue.

Copyable input or command

cd backend
chmod +x mvnw
./mvnw spring-boot:run

# Windows PowerShell instead:
# .\mvnw.cmd spring-boot:run

Expected result

The backend listens at http://localhost:18707. Local account data is in backend/data.

If your screen differs

“No POM” means the directory is wrong. “Port 18707 already in use” means another process owns the port. Stop your earlier copy before retrying. Use the current complete Practice ZIP if an older package is installed.

05 / Start Terminal B and open Vue

01 / Setup

Where to begin

A new terminal at campus-board, separate from Terminal A.

Do this, in order

  1. Run cd frontend, then npm ci. The command installs the versions recorded in package-lock.json.
  2. Run npm run dev. Read the Local URL printed by Vite and open it in the browser. It is normally http://localhost:15707.
  3. Keep Terminal A and B running at the same time. A page loading by itself does not prove that its API can be reached.
  4. Visit http://localhost:18707/actuator/health separately. Look for status UP, then visit /api/posts and expect an empty array on a fresh database.

Copyable input or command

cd frontend
npm ci
npm run dev

Expected result

The sign-in form and an empty board appear. API health is UP.

If your screen differs

“Failed to fetch” or a Vite proxy error usually means Java is stopped. A missing package.json means you are outside frontend. Use npm run dev for this local path, not npm run preview.

06 / Run the complete application

02 / Local practice

Where to begin

The local Vue page at http://localhost:15707.

Do this, in order

  1. Check that the API health endpoint reports UP and the page loads.
  2. Register Alex, sign in, then publish and edit a post.
  3. Create Sam in a private browser window. Find Alex’s post and observe the author-only controls.
  4. Run the supplied backend and frontend tests, then continue with cloud configuration and Swagger checks. No source-code implementation is required.

Expected result

The supplied app supports signup, login, and author-only changes.

If your screen differs

Keep both terminals running. Check the page URL, API health, and the first terminal error if a step fails. Code explanations are optional reading in the Code Walkthrough.

07 / Fill all four registration fields

02 / Local practice

Where to begin

Vue: New here? Create an account.

Do this, in order

  1. Enter Name: Alex and Email: alex.walkthrough@example.com. These are fictional classroom values; use a fresh address if you already created that account.
  2. Enter PracticeOnly123! into Password and Confirm password. This public example password is only for the disposable exercise.
  3. Click Create account once. Wait for the request to finish. The form disables its button while it is busy.
  4. Wait for the confirmation, then sign in with the account you just created.

Expected result

Registration succeeds and the form returns to sign-in.

If your screen differs

A confirmation mismatch is a browser form problem. 400 is server validation. 409 means that email already exists. Changing only the display name does not create another account with the same email.

08 / Read the registration confirmation

02 / Local practice

Where to begin

Vue: the form after Create account finishes.

Do this, in order

  1. Look for “Account created. Sign in with your password.” The account now exists in the database.
  2. The email remains in the form. Enter the same password again and click Sign in.
  3. Registration and login are separate requests. Do not assume that creating an account automatically supplies an access token in this sample.

Expected result

A successful login changes the sidebar to the signed-in user and the post form.

If your screen differs

If the address already exists, use sign-in rather than repeatedly creating the same account.

09 / Try one wrong password deliberately

02 / Local practice

Where to begin

Vue: sign-in form.

Do this, in order

  1. Keep the correct email. Enter WrongPractice123! and click Sign in.
  2. Read the inline error. It should say that the email or password is incorrect. The post form should remain unavailable.
  3. Replace it with the correct classroom password and sign in again. The successful /me request confirms the identity accepted by the server.

Expected result

Wrong credentials fail; correct credentials reveal the account and post form.

If your screen differs

If the password is correct but the following /me request is 401, sign in again and inspect the Authorization header. The login request itself can succeed while the protected request lacks its header.

10 / Publish the first post

02 / Local practice

Where to begin

Vue: Signed in as Alex, A new post.

Do this, in order

  1. Enter Title: Thursday study group.
  2. Enter Message: Bring one interface you like. Meet at the library at 3 PM.
  3. Click Publish post. Wait until the button becomes available again and the public list refreshes.
  4. The request sends title and content. It does not send ownerId. The backend gets the author from the verified token.

Expected result

A new card appears under The latest, with Your post, Edit, and Delete.

If your screen differs

An empty title or message prevents a valid submission. If the UI shows a session error, sign in again before publishing.

11 / Check the stored result

02 / Local practice

Where to begin

Vue: The latest, after publishing.

Do this, in order

  1. Check that the title and message match what you entered.
  2. Notice Your post and the Edit/Delete buttons. This account owns this record.
  3. Click Edit. The existing text should move into the form. You are editing the selected post, not creating a duplicate.

Expected result

The form heading changes to Edit your post and its submit button becomes Save changes.

If your screen differs

If the card is missing, use Refresh and check the API response. A successful POST returns 201.

12 / Save a change to the existing post

02 / Local practice

Where to begin

Vue: Edit your post.

Do this, in order

  1. Change the title to Thursday study group / updated. Keep the message or edit it.
  2. Click Save changes and wait for the updated title to appear in the list.
  3. To abandon an edit before saving, use Cancel editing. This does not send a PUT request.

Expected result

The same post has the updated title. The form returns to A new post.

If your screen differs

A 403 means the signed-in account is not the stored author. A 404 means the record no longer exists. Do not handle these by silently creating a new post.

13 / Separate browser state from stored data

02 / Local practice

Where to begin

Vue: reload the browser page.

Do this, in order

  1. Reload once. The sidebar returns to Welcome back because the token was stored only in memory.
  2. Look at The latest. The updated post is still present because the server database stores it.
  3. Sign in again when you need to write. This local reload test is different from replacing a deployed application container.

Expected result

The account is signed out in the browser, but the post remains.

If your screen differs

A blank board after a cloud redeployment needs a database/profile check. A sign-in form after a reload is expected and does not mean the database was erased.

14 / Use a second account to inspect the same post

02 / Local practice

Where to begin

Vue: a private window, or sign out and sign in as Sam.

Do this, in order

  1. Create Sam using sam.walkthrough@example.com and a classroom password. Keep Alex’s account separate.
  2. Sign in as Sam and read Alex’s updated post. You should see the public content.
  3. Check that Edit and Delete are absent on Alex’s card. Sam can still create a different post.
  4. This is a UI check. In the final Swagger chapter you will send PUT and DELETE directly as Sam and prove that the server also rejects them.

Expected result

Sam can read Alex’s content but cannot use author-only controls on it.

If your screen differs

If you accidentally log in as Alex again, the buttons will still appear. Read the sidebar name and email before drawing a conclusion.

15 / Run the same checks before you push

03 / Verification

Where to begin

Terminal in each named folder.

Do this, in order

  1. In backend, run ./mvnw test (Windows: .\mvnw.cmd test). The completed sample has 9 integration test methods.
  2. In frontend, run npm test and npm run build. The request helper has 4 tests, and Vite should produce dist.
  3. With Java running, open another terminal at campus-board and run the smoke script below. It exercises the actual HTTP service.
  4. Read PASS 403 as a successful denial check, not a broken test. The script creates two practice accounts and deletes its own test post.

Copyable input or command

node scripts/smoke.mjs http://localhost:18707

Expected result

All tests and the frontend build succeed. The smoke script ends with All checks passed.

If your screen differs

The supplied complete project should pass all checks. Read the first failed assertion if a check fails. Never bypass failing security tests with -DskipTests when deploying.

16 / Create your cloud-service accounts

04 / Deployment preparation

Where to begin

The official signup links below.

Do this, in order

  1. GitHub: create an account for your repository. Complete the verification shown by the site, or sign in if you already have an account.
  2. Neon: create an account or sign in, then open the console and create the database project.
  3. Render: create an account or sign in, then connect the GitHub account that owns your campus-board repository.
  4. Choose Free when creating the lab resources. These accounts are separate from the Alex and Sam accounts used inside Campus Board.

Account signup links

Already have an account? Sign in. Complete any requested verification, then continue to the dashboard.

  • GitHub — Host the project repository. https://github.com/signup
  • Neon — Create the PostgreSQL database. https://console.neon.tech/signup
  • Render — Build and run the web service. https://dashboard.render.com/register

These are cloud-service accounts. The Alex and Sam practice accounts are created separately in Campus Board.

Expected result

You can access GitHub, the Neon console, and the Render dashboard.

If your screen differs

If the page redirects to a dashboard, you may already be signed in. Check the account you are using before creating the repository or service.

17 / Create the database project in Neon

04 / Database

Where to begin

https://console.neon.tech/ after your own sign-in.

Do this, in order

  1. Use your own Neon account. If this is the first visit, complete onboarding, then choose New project or the project creation action shown by the console.
  2. Name the project campus-board. Choose the Free plan. Pick a region near the Render region you intend to use.
  3. Keep the offered default PostgreSQL version, database, and role unless your instructor provides different values. The sample was tested against PostgreSQL 17.
  4. Create the project and wait until the console shows the project overview. You do not need to create app_user or post manually: Flyway creates them when the app first starts.

Expected result

A project exists and its navigation offers Connect.

If your screen differs

This pack does not contain a live Neon database. If the account requires verification, complete it yourself. Do not choose a paid plan merely to bypass a setup issue.

Official reference: https://neon.com/docs/get-started/signing-up

18 / Open Connect to your branch

04 / Database

Where to begin

Neon project navigation: Connect.

Do this, in order

  1. Open Connect. The dialog title is Connect to your branch. Select the branch that will store your classroom data.
  2. Choose the Postgres database tab. Keep the primary compute, choose the intended database, and read the selected Role.
  3. For this small Spring Boot + Flyway lab, turn Connection pooling OFF. The official example image shows it ON, so you must change that switch in your own console.
  4. Confirm that the resulting direct hostname does not contain -pooler. The project, branch, role, and database can differ from the example image.

Expected result

The dialog gives a direct PostgreSQL connection string for your chosen database.

If your screen differs

Do not copy a hostname from a screenshot. Use the values from your own project. Auth, Data API, and Storage tabs do not provide the JDBC database credentials for this backend.

Official reference: https://neon.com/docs/connect/connect-from-any-app

19 / Find host, database, role, and password

04 / Database

Where to begin

Neon: Connect to your branch, connection string area.

Do this, in order

  1. Read the Role selector for DB_USERNAME and the Database selector for the database name.
  2. Use Show password to reveal the role password only when you need to transfer it to your own service. Do not press Reset password to merely view it.
  3. The hostname starts after @ and ends before /DATABASE. Copy this complete hostname, including its region and domain.
  4. If copying a connection URL rather than separate fields, distinguish the role/password segment from the hostname. The final Java URL will not include role:password@.

Expected result

You have four values from the same project, branch, database, and role.

If your screen differs

A masked ******** value is not a usable password. A percent-encoded password in a URI may differ from its raw value. Prefer copying the actual password field/display for DB_PASSWORD.

Official reference: https://neon.com/docs/connect/connect-from-any-app

20 / Map the connection to three Render values

04 / Database

Where to begin

A private note on your own computer, then Render Environment.

Do this, in order

  1. Build DB_URL as jdbc:postgresql://HOST/DATABASE?sslmode=require. Replace HOST and DATABASE with the values you just selected.
  2. Put the selected role in DB_USERNAME and the raw role password in DB_PASSWORD. No quotes are needed in Render fields.
  3. Keep the jdbc: prefix. The postgresql:// string from Neon by itself is not the Java JDBC format used here.
  4. The names DB_URL, DB_USERNAME, and DB_PASSWORD come from this project’s application-prod.yml. Do not rename them to DATABASE_URL just because another tutorial uses that name.

Copyable input or command

DB_URL=jdbc:postgresql://YOUR_DIRECT_HOST/YOUR_DATABASE?sslmode=require
DB_USERNAME=YOUR_ROLE
DB_PASSWORD=YOUR_PASSWORD

Expected result

The three fields describe one matching database connection.

If your screen differs

Pasting an entire psql command, including its shell quotes, into DB_URL prevents startup. Keep passwords out of source files and screenshots.

21 / Prepare an empty GitHub repository

05 / Repository

Where to begin

https://github.com/new after signing in.

Do this, in order

  1. Choose your own account in Owner. The account or organization shown in this capture is only an example.
  2. Enter campus-board as the repository name, or use another unused name. The screenshot uses campus-board-week07 as a form example.
  3. Private is suitable if Render has permission to read that repository. Keep No template, Add README off, No .gitignore, and No license, because the extracted project already supplies its files.
  4. Create the repository in your account. Copy its HTTPS URL from the empty repository page. Creating the repository alone does not upload your local project.

Expected result

You have an empty repository URL in your own account.

If your screen differs

Do not copy the example account name. If you initialized a README on GitHub, the repository is no longer empty; reconcile that history instead of force-pushing over it.

Official reference: https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/creating-a-new-repository

22 / Push the project root, not its parent folder

05 / Repository

Where to begin

Terminal at campus-board, where Dockerfile is visible.

Do this, in order

  1. Run git init and git branch -M main. If Git asks for identity, set user.name and user.email in this repository.
  2. Run git add . and inspect git status --short before committing. You should see source and configuration, but no node_modules, target, backend/data, real .env, or credentials.
  3. Commit the files. Replace the remote URL in the command with the actual HTTPS URL copied from your own GitHub repository.
  4. Push and complete GitHub’s normal authentication flow. Refresh GitHub. Dockerfile, backend, and frontend should appear directly at the repository root.

Copyable input or command

git init
git branch -M main
git add .
git status --short
git commit -m "Complete week 7 practice"
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR_ACCOUNT/campus-board.git
git push -u origin main

Expected result

The main branch contains the completed project and package-lock.json.

If your screen differs

If Git reports an existing remote, use git remote -v to check it. “Repository not found” can mean a wrong URL or missing private-repository access. A rejected push is not a reason to use --force.

25 / Set the Java service to Docker

06 / Render

Where to begin

Render creation form: Name, Language, Branch, Region.

Do this, in order

  1. Choose a unique Name. The final service hostname will be shown by Render after creation.
  2. Open Language and choose Docker. It can be selected even though Java does not appear as a native language option.

26 / Select Free and verify the amount

06 / Render

Where to begin

Render creation form: Compute.

Do this, in order

  1. Click the Free option labelled $0 / month. The inspected form initially selected a paid $7/month option, so check this explicitly.
  2. Read the selected summary. It should say $0 / month, 0.1 CPU, and 512 MB RAM on the captured plan.
  3. Read the idle/sleep notice. A free instance can take time to wake after inactivity. These limitations are expected for this classroom exercise.

Expected result

The selected compute and the bottom action bar show $0 / month.

If the displayed amount is not zero, stop and review the plan. Free availability, quotas, or verification requirements may change.

27 / Enter all five environment variables

06 / Render

Where to begin

Render creation form: Environment Variables.

Do this, in order

  1. First row: Key SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE, Value prod. Add the next row with Add Environment Variable.
  2. Add DB_URL, DB_USERNAME, and DB_PASSWORD using the Neon values from the previous section.
  3. Generate JWT_SECRET with the Node command below on your own machine. Add the output as the fifth value. It must be your fresh Base64 value, not the placeholder in the screenshot.
  4. Count five rows and check spelling. Do not include quotation marks around dashboard values. Never put these real values in Vue files or GitHub.

Copyable input or command

node -e "console.log(require('node:crypto').randomBytes(32).toString('base64'))"

Expected result

The five exact keys are present and every placeholder has been replaced in your own service.

If your screen differs

A .env.example file is a checklist, not an automatic Render configuration. JWT_SECRET must decode to at least 32 bytes. A missing prod profile can use the wrong database settings.

28 / Set the health check in Advanced

06 / Render

Where to begin

Render creation form: expand Advanced.

Do this, in order

  1. Find Health Check Path and enter /actuator/health exactly, including the leading slash.
  2. Keep Docker Command blank. The supplied Dockerfile already starts java -jar and reads the Render PORT variable through Spring configuration.
  3. Keep Docker Build Context Directory at the repository root. Check Dockerfile Path again if the form shows it in both basic and advanced settings.
  4. Review repository, branch, Docker, Free, all five variables, and health path before selecting Deploy web service in your own account.

Expected result

Render will check the application health endpoint rather than only whether a web page loads.

If your screen differs

Do not enter a full https:// URL as the path. A failing health check can mean a database connection problem even when the Java process has started.

Official reference: https://render.com/docs/health-checks

29 / Follow the deployment log stage by stage

06 / Render

Where to begin

Your Render service: Events and Logs after Deploy web service.

Do this, in order

  1. Wait for the Node build stage: npm ci followed by npm run build. A missing lock file stops this stage.
  2. Next, Maven downloads Java dependencies, runs tests, and creates the executable JAR. A failing ownership test should stop the deployment.
  3. At runtime, look for the PostgreSQL connection, Flyway migration, and “Started BoardApplication”. The health check must pass before treating the release as ready.
  4. If deployment fails, read the earliest meaningful error in that failed stage. Correct the configuration or code, then deploy again. Do not repeatedly create new services.

Expected result

Render marks the service ready/live and provides an HTTPS onrender.com URL.

If your screen differs

No successful Render deployment was performed during these captures. These are the steps to run in your own account. The screenshots of creation forms are not proof of a completed cloud deployment.

Official reference: https://render.com/docs/deploys

30 / Check the public URL in three places

06 / Render

Where to begin

Your assigned Render HTTPS address.

Do this, in order

  1. Open the root URL and check that the Vue board loads.
  2. Append /actuator/health and expect {"status":"UP"}. Then open /api/posts and expect a JSON array.
  3. Register fresh cloud accounts and create a practice post. Local H2 users are not copied into Neon automatically.
  4. Run node scripts/smoke.mjs with the actual HTTPS URL. After an application redeploy, sign in again and verify that the same post remains.

Copyable input or command

node scripts/smoke.mjs https://YOUR_SERVICE.onrender.com

Expected result

The public UI, API, authorization checks, and database persistence work together.

If your screen differs

A slow first request after sleep is different from a repeated startup failure. Check logs and health before retrying. A page loading does not prove that writes or ownership checks work.

31 / Open the explorer and find the actual response

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Local: http://localhost:18707/swagger-ui.html. Cloud: your Render URL plus /swagger-ui.html.

Do this, in order

  1. Expand an operation by clicking its method/path row. Click Try it out to enable inputs.
  2. Enter values that meet the API rules. Click Execute once and wait for Server response.
  3. Read Code and the actual Response body under Server response. The lower Example Value panel only shows a schema example and does not prove a request ran.
  4. The captures use a local verification port. Use your own localhost:18707 or public service URL while following the same operations.

Expected result

You can distinguish generated examples from a real response.

If your screen differs

Swagger writes affect the same database used by Vue. Use fictional classroom data. The generated Curl command can contain a token after authorization, so keep it out of shared screenshots.

32 / Call /me before you authorize

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Swagger: GET /api/me.

Do this, in order

  1. If a previous token is set, open Authorize, choose Logout, and close the dialog.
  2. Expand GET /api/me, click Try it out, then Execute. There is no request body.
  3. Read Code 401 and the UNAUTHENTICATED error. This proves that the endpoint requires a valid token.

Expected result

401 with a message asking you to sign in using a valid, unexpired token.

If your screen differs

Swagger may label this error Undocumented because the operation schema lists its main response. The actual HTTP status and JSON body are still the real server result.

33 / Create the second account through Swagger

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Swagger: POST /api/auth/signup.

Do this, in order

  1. Click Try it out and replace the entire sample JSON with the values below.
  2. Click Execute. For a new email, look for Code 201 and a response with id, name, and email.
  3. Use a new email if the same one was already created through Vue. Save the practice email/password locally so the later login uses the same pair.

Copyable input or command

{"name":"Sam","email":"sam.walkthrough@example.com","password":"PracticeOnly123!"}

Expected result

201 Created with a safe user profile, without a password hash.

If your screen differs

Leaving the password as string fails the length rule. A name/email field with an invalid value can return 400.

34 / Verify the 201 profile

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Swagger: actual Server response from signup.

Do this, in order

  1. Check Code 201 rather than only the example listed at the bottom.
  2. Read the returned UUID. This is a user ID, not a post ID.
  3. Confirm the response has no password and no passwordHash.

Expected result

The account exists and can now attempt login.

If your screen differs

Do not copy a user ID into the post {id} field later. A post receives a different UUID when you create it.

35 / Execute the same signup again

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Swagger: same signup input, second Execute.

Do this, in order

  1. Keep the same email and click Execute again.
  2. Read the new Server response. A duplicate account should return 409.
  3. Continue with login for the existing account instead of changing its password in the signup form.

Expected result

409 CONFLICT and a duplicate-account message.

If your screen differs

A database restart in the normal local profile does not erase backend/data. Reusing the email after restarting can still be a valid duplicate.

36 / Log in and copy only accessToken

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Swagger: POST /api/auth/login.

Do this, in order

  1. Expand login, choose Try it out, and enter the same email and password used for registration.
  2. Click Execute and confirm 200. In the actual Response body, find the accessToken property.
  3. Copy only the characters inside the accessToken string. Do not copy surrounding quotes, tokenType, the whole JSON object, or a line break.
  4. The capture shows only the status area. Token contents are intentionally excluded. Use the fresh token returned by your own request.

Copyable input or command

{"email":"sam.walkthrough@example.com","password":"PracticeOnly123!"}

Expected result

A 200 response contains accessToken, tokenType, expiresIn, and user.

If your screen differs

A token from a previous local server run may fail because the local signing key changes at restart. Log in again.

37 / Apply the token in Authorize

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Swagger: top-level Authorize button.

Do this, in order

  1. Open Authorize and find bearerAuth (http, Bearer).
  2. Paste only the token into Value. This scheme adds “Bearer ” itself.
  3. Click Authorize, then Close. A locked icon indicates configured authorization, but the next /me request is the real validity check.
  4. When switching accounts, choose Logout in this dialog first and apply the new account’s token. Calling login alone does not replace the authorized token.

Expected result

Protected operations can include the Authorization header.

If your screen differs

“Bearer Bearer …” fails. Avoid copying the whole response object. Do not include a real token in shared screenshots.

38 / Confirm that Sam is the requester

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Swagger: GET /api/me after Authorize.

Do this, in order

  1. Execute /api/me again. Read Code 200.
  2. Check the name and email in the actual response. The captured call belongs to Sam.
  3. If the response says Alex while you intend to test Sam, replace the authorization token before testing ownership.

Expected result

200 with the exact account whose token was applied.

If your screen differs

A padlock icon alone does not verify the token or reveal which user it belongs to. The response is the evidence.

39 / Find Alex’s post ID in the list

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Swagger: GET /api/posts.

Do this, in order

  1. Execute the public list endpoint and locate Alex’s title.
  2. Copy that object’s id value. Do not copy ownerId. The id identifies the post; ownerId identifies its author.
  3. Keep this post ID while Sam remains the authorized requester.

Expected result

You have a real post ID that belongs to another account.

If your screen differs

Do not use the schema’s example UUID. It is not guaranteed to exist in your database.

40 / Send Sam’s request to Alex’s post

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Swagger: PUT /api/posts/{id}.

Do this, in order

  1. Click Try it out. Paste Alex’s post id into the id path parameter.
  2. Replace the request body with a different title and content. This endpoint expects both editable fields.
  3. Click Execute while /me still identifies Sam. A manually constructed request must not bypass author checks.

Copyable input or command

{"title":"Sam tries to edit this","content":"This request must fail."}

Expected result

The server returns 403 and keeps the original post unchanged.

If your screen differs

If you get 404, first check the copied post ID. If you get 401, fix authorization before testing ownership.

41 / Read the actual 403 result

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Swagger: Server response after Sam’s PUT.

Do this, in order

  1. Check Code 403 and the FORBIDDEN response.
  2. Execute GET /api/posts/{id} or refresh Vue and confirm that Alex’s original title remains.
  3. The denial occurs in the backend. It does not depend on the Vue Edit button being hidden.

Expected result

403 with “Only the author can change this post.”

If your screen differs

If the edit succeeds, inspect requireOwner and the user ID supplied by the controller. Treat that as a failed security checkpoint.

42 / Repeat the denial check for DELETE

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Swagger: DELETE /api/posts/{id}, still authorized as Sam.

Do this, in order

  1. Paste the same Alex post ID and Execute.
  2. Expect 403 again. GET the post afterward and confirm it still exists.
  3. Update and delete must enforce the same ownership rule. Passing only one of these checks is incomplete.

Expected result

403 and the original record remains readable.

If your screen differs

Do not switch to Alex’s token until both forbidden requests have been verified.

43 / Try an empty title as an authenticated user

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Swagger: POST /api/posts.

Do this, in order

  1. With a valid token, send title as an empty string and content as a nonempty message.
  2. Execute and read 400 INVALID_INPUT.
  3. Fix the title and execute again. A valid new post should then return 201.

Copyable input or command

{"title":"","content":"Title is deliberately empty."}

Expected result

Invalid JSON field values fail before a post is stored.

If your screen differs

401 points to authentication, not title validation. Make sure /me succeeds before testing the body.

44 / Create a disposable post as Sam

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Swagger: POST /api/posts, with a valid title and content.

Do this, in order

  1. Use a title such as Sam temporary API test and a short classroom message.
  2. Execute and read Code 201. Copy the new post id from the actual response.
  3. This record belongs to Sam, so it is the correct one for the successful DELETE test below.

Expected result

201 with an id and ownerId for the newly stored record.

If your screen differs

Keep this ID separate from Alex’s ID. Deleting Alex’s post as Sam must continue to fail.

45 / Delete the post owned by the current user

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Swagger: DELETE /api/posts/{id}.

Do this, in order

  1. Use the ID of Sam’s disposable post, not Alex’s ID.
  2. Execute with Sam’s token. Read Code 204.
  3. 204 has no response body. An empty body is the expected success result.

Expected result

The post has been removed and no JSON body is returned.

If your screen differs

The frontend helper handles 204 before JSON parsing. Trying to parse an empty body can create a client error after a successful deletion.

46 / Read the deleted ID once more

07 / Swagger

Where to begin

Swagger: GET /api/posts/{id}.

Do this, in order

  1. Use the same Sam post ID after the successful deletion.
  2. Execute and expect 404 NOT_FOUND.
  3. Record the complete sequence: POST 201, DELETE 204, then GET 404. Keep the separate 403 checks for Alex’s post.

Expected result

404 confirms that the record no longer exists.

If your screen differs

A 404 before deleting may mean the wrong ID was copied. The sequence and the account identity make the evidence meaningful.
